data.title: New York State Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins dies at 76
data.description:
Video above features Stewart-Cousins taking about environmental legislation in February.

ALBANY, N.Y. (NEWS10) — New York State Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins died on Friday. She was 76. Senate Majority Communications Director Mike Murphy announced her passing.

“Serving the people of the 35th Senate District was one of the greatest honors of her life,” said Murphy. “Throughout her decades in public service, Stewart-Cousins made a profound impact on the lives of New Yorkers. She was a groundbreaking leader who shattered one of New York’s highest glass ceilings, becoming the first woman to lead the New York State Senate.”

Stewart-Cousins was the longest-serving Democratic Majority Leader in state senate history. She was also the first African American woman to have the role. She was elected to the state senate in 2006.

During her tenure, Stewart-Cousins focused on reproductive rights, women’s health rights, and education. She was born and raised in New York and was a resident of Yonkers. Before the senate, she served as a Westchester County Legislator and was the first African American Director of Community Affairs for Yonkers. 

Stewart-Cousins is survived by her brother, Robert Stewart Jr., her three children, Kevin, Steven, and Candice, and her six grandchildren. She was preceded in death by her husband, Thomas Cousins.

“We ask that you keep Majority Leader Stewart-Cousins’ family, friends, and staff in your thoughts and prayers during this difficult time,” said Murphy. “Information regarding memorial services and public tributes will be shared in the coming days.”

New York State Governor Kathy Hochul said that Stewart-Cousins was a dear friend. Hochul said she’ll never forget introducing her as the Majority Leader for the first time in 2019.

“I knew how hard she had worked to get there and how many women had dreamed of seeing that day. Andrea made history that day, and every day that followed, she made that history mean something,” said Hochul. “Andrea possessed a rare combination of quiet grace and extraordinary strength. She never forgot where she came from, who she was fighting for or the doors she could open for those coming behind her.”

“During my time in Albany, I have always respected and appreciated her partnership, dignity and demeanor. While we didn’t always agree on policy, we shared a common belief in the value and importance of public service and the work we did on behalf of New Yorkers,” said Senate Republican Leader Rob Ortt. “As the first woman Senate Majority Leader, Andrea Stewart-Cousins leaves a lasting legacy in the halls of the State Capitol.”

New York State Sen-Elect Aber Kawas was recently sworn-in by Stewart-Cousins to represent Queens District 12. She told NEWS10’s Sarah Willson that she was shocked by the news of her passing.

“She was truly at a high, celebrating all of he achievements of having a huge caucus of 48, which was more than she imagined,” said Kawas. “It really is sad to have lost her in this moment.”

“The Leader had the energy of ten, and led with a powerful strength that began with her extraordinary, dignified presence, manner, and speech,” said State Senator Pat Fahy. “It is impossible to comprehend how she will be replaced. Not only was she the longest-serving Leader, she had the utmost respect from every member of the Senate on both sides of the aisle. Her leadership was unquestioned and her character beyond reproach.”

“As the first African American woman to lead a legislative conference in Albany, Sen. Stewart-Cousins left an indelible mark on New York State and set a historic standard for others to emulate,” said Assembly Minority Leader Ed Ra.”While our policy perspectives differed, I respected her professionalism, thoughtfulness and the historic achievements that defined her career.”

data.title: Sen. Deb Fischer's office says her husband died by suicide
data.description:
A spokesperson for Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.) said Friday her husband, Bruce Fischer, whose death was announced earlier in the week, had died by suicide.

“There has been a sad update in the death of Senator Fischer’s husband, Bruce,” the spokesperson, who did not offer their name, said in a statement. “Initially, it was believed that Bruce passed peacefully at home.

“Upon further investigation, it was learned that Bruce chose to end his life. The family is deeply grateful for the recent outpouring of sympathy for their loss, and asks for understanding in this time of mourning. There will be no further comment and no other details will be provided.”

The Nebraska senator announced her husband’s death on Monday, saying he died the day before.

“Bruce was my partner in life, my greatest source of strength, and the heart of our family. His kindness, integrity, and quiet strength left a lasting impression on all who knew him,” she said in a statement.

Fischer had said her husband “passed away peacefully while doing what he loved most, spending time outdoors,” adding her family “is heartbroken by his passing, but we find comfort in the life we shared.”

She added, “I will cherish the decades we spent building a family in the Nebraska Sandhills. Above all, Bruce was a loving husband, a devoted father and grandfather, a man of faith and a rancher.”

Deb Fischer, 75, is in her third term representing Nebraska in the upper chamber. Prior to her time in the Senate, she spent eight years in the Nebraska Legislature.

The senator and her husband married in 1972, after they met while attending the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, according to the Lincoln Journal Star. They raised three sons, the outlet reported.

Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.), who has represented Nebraska alongside Deb Fischer since 2023, said Monday he was “very sad” to hear of Bruce Fischer’s death.

“Bruce left his mark on this world through his love for family, his faith, and his ranch,” Ricketts wrote on the social platform X, adding that he and his wife Susanne “send our deepest condolences to Deb, the entire Fischer family, and all their loved ones during this difficult time.”

If you or someone you know is experiencing mental health struggles, contact the 988 Suicide & Crisis lifeline by calling or texting “988.”

data.title: Thousands still without power after Thanksgiving storms
data.description:
Thousands of households in the U.S. were without power on Black Friday after storms hit both the Northeast and West Coast on Thanksgiving.

Roughly 490,000 customers were without power as of Friday afternoon, according to tracking website PowerOutage.us. That included nearly 201,000 in New Jersey and Pennsylvania, about 69,500 in Missouri, roughly 60,000 in Maryland and more than 40,000 in New York, where the storms had postponed the famous Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade until Saturday.

Power outages on Thanksgiving peaked at 940,000 customers, NBC News reported — citing data from PowerOutage.us.

Airlines have delayed nearly 1,950 flights within, into or out of the U.S. so far Friday, according to flight tracking site FlightAware. Airlines have also cancelled nearly 130 U.S. flights, although it is unclear what percentage of the delayed and cancelled flights were impacted by weather.

Conditions across the Eastern part of the country will “begin to improve” on Friday, the National Weather Service’s (NWS) prediction center said in an early morning statement.

“Seasonably cool temperatures will be felt across the Southeast in wake of the storm system before moderating this weekend,” the NWS said. “Rounds of rain along the coastline and valleys and locally heavy snow in high terrain will occur across the Pacific Northwest and portions of the northern Rockies Friday and Saturday.”

A storm system that moved from Florida through the Carolinas and to the Northeast brought inclement weather again on Friday, the service added. The system brought wet snow as far south as the Tennessee Valley.

data.title: Keep the filibuster, but make senators earn it
data.description:
Ask most Americans what a filibuster looks like and they will describe Jimmy Stewart in “Mr. Smith Goes to Washington”: a lone senator on his feet, hoarse and unshaven, refusing to yield the floor until the nation has heard him out. It is a good image. It is also fiction, and not only because it is a movie.

Until the early 1970s, senators who wanted to stop a bill had to hold the floor and talk. Today a senator need only send an email to the majority leader threatening a filibuster. That tells the leader the Senate will need 60 votes before it can even begin to discuss the bill. In practice, the bill never reaches the floor, no one has to explain why, and the public never learns who put on the brakes.

The world’s greatest deliberative body has ground to a halt, which is why calls to abolish the filibuster now come from all sides. President Trump wants it gone. So do several newly elected Democratic senators, among them Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) and James Talarico (D-Texas).

But abolition gets the diagnosis wrong. The problem is not that the Senate protects unlimited debate. The problem is that the Senate no longer requires any debate. The minority can block legislation without accountability. It should earn that right on the floor, not from behind a computer screen.

Accountability runs in both directions. A majority should not be able to silence the minority with a timer, and a minority should not be able to stop the majority from governing with an email.

To get there, two fixes are needed. The first is the talking filibuster, which Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) has advocated for more than a decade: if you want to block a vote, you hold the floor. You may take turns. You may speak for weeks. But you must talk.

The second is the burden of proof. Today the majority must produce 60 votes to move forward, while the minority produces nothing. The solution, which the political scientist Norman Ornstein has long urged, is to flip it: the opponents should show they have the votes to keep debating. If they cannot, debate ends, and a majority vote follows.

Together, these two fixes mean the 41 senators who can now suffocate a bill from their offices would have to come to the floor, make their case, and be counted, again and again. The moment they stopped doing either, the Senate would vote.

Consider the kill switch at work on the Tax Relief for American Families and Workers Act in 2024. In January it passed the House 357-70. On Aug. 1, a motion to take it up drew 48 votes in favor and 44 against, a majority. It died without discussion. The senators who blocked it were back in their offices within the hour. That is not democracy.

To be sure, a determined minority could still hold the floor for a long time, and the majority would have to keep the Senate in session to outlast it. That is a real cost. It is also the point. Obstruction should reflect conviction, not convenience. And most of these fights would end not in exhaustion but in negotiation, because a stalemate the public can watch costs both sides. The silent filibuster makes compromise unnecessary. The talking filibuster makes it attractive.

The usual objection is that Senate rules can be changed only by a two-thirds vote that a divided chamber will never produce. Yet in 2013, a Democratic majority established by simple majority that most nominations could no longer be filibustered. In 2017, a Republican majority extended that to the Supreme Court. Each was done by a point of order sustained by 51 senators, and each is now settled practice. A talking filibuster could be adopted the same way.

It is understandable that freshman senators will be tempted to end the filibuster. It stands in the way of what they promised to do. But someday, they or their successors will be in the minority and will want a way to make the majority listen.

A new Congress will be seated in January, when the rules can be reset. The question I would put to every senator is this: Would you accept this reformed filibuster from your opponents when your party is in the minority? If so, support it now, while the question is still about the institution rather than the next vote.

Mr. Smith had it right. Let the senators talk. Let the minority make its case. Let it earn its delay. But if they stop talking, let the Senate vote.

John P. Giraudo is a lawyer and a Henry Crown Fellow of the Aspen Institute.

data.title: Trump to visit groundbreaking for semiconductor manufacturer that supplies Nvidia: Reports
data.description:
President Trump is reportedly set to visit the groundbreaking of a Phoenix facility that will manufacture semiconductor chips, including for Nvidia, which has seized the spotlight this month over the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang.

A White House official told multiple outlets that Trump will tour and deliver remarks at a Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) plant next Friday.

TSMC unveiled plans to expand into Arizona in 2020, saying at the time it would spend roughly $12 billion from 2021 to 2029 on the project. 

The Hill has reached out to the White House and TSMC for comment.

Trump’s visit will come following Nvidia reinstatement of Huang as CEO after the president’s urging.

In announcing the reinstatement of Huang, who resigned on Nov. 12 amid reports about his extramarital affairs — including one with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang — Nvidia’s board argued his return did not pose any national security risks, citing conversations with “senior levels” of the U.S. government.

“And I must tell you, it was a lot easier to convince them yesterday than it was a week and a half ago,” Trump said of the board on CNBC, referencing Nvidia’s falling stock price.

While Nvidia shares saw a Huang-fueled bump on Monday, they have since declined and closed at $150.49 on Black Friday.

Nvidia’s stock, while above last Friday’s closing mark of $125.53 per share, is nearly $93 below where it stood on Oct. 6 — when it reached an all-time high of $243.37 per share.

Trump did not rule out pardoning Huang on Tuesday, although he told The New York Post he did not think it would be “necessary.”

data.title: Cenk Uygur backs Ro Khanna in 2028 race
data.description:
Progressive media personality Cenk Uygur on Thursday backed Rep. Ro Khanna as a candidate in the 2028 presidential race, if the California Democrat decides to run.

“So, 2028 presidential campaign starts right now. I endorse Representative Ro Khanna for president of the United States of America. So, there’s a couple reasons why I’m endorsing him. Number one, he’s the — I think — going to be the only populist in the race on the Democratic side, and he is a progressive. I’m a left-wing populist, so it makes sense,” Uygur said on the Twitch stream of his nephew, Hasan Piker, another notable left-wing personality.

“He’s already proven himself. Got the Epstein files released. Showed incredible — both bravery and action and leadership. Is the most in favor of ending this [Iran] war. He’s for zeroing out aid to Israel. He’s called [Israel’s actions in the Gaza war] a genocide. I think those are litmus tests. We can come back to those issues. And, you know, most importantly, he’s going to win,” he added.

Politico was the first to report on the endorsement from Uygur.

Earlier this month, allies of Khanna launched an effort to press him to run for the White House.

Heading up the “Run Ro” draft committee are former Rep. Jamaal Bowman (D-N.Y.) and progressive political activist Nomiki Konst, per a news release shared with The Hill’s sister network NewsNation.

The committee also features members of former President Obama’s and Sen. Bernie Sanders’s (I-Vt.) presidential campaigns.

Khanna has not officially announced a bid for the White House, though he has publicly weighed a bid.

The Hill has reached out to Khanna’s office for comment.

The California Democrat has been in the political spotlight in the last two years, co-leading an effort alongside Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) to release files linked to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The 2028 Democratic presidential primary is expected to be a crowded one, particularly in the wake of this month’s sweeping midterm election victories for the party.

data.title: 14 years of DACA isn't a milestone — it's a failure of Congress
data.description:
Fourteen years ago, the Department of Homeland Security established the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals or DACA program. It was designed to provide, temporarily, hundreds of thousands of young immigrants who were raised, educated and deeply rooted in the U.S. with protection from deportation, and to give them the ability to work legally. It was never meant to be a permanent solution, but a stopgap measure taken via executive action in the face of congressional inaction.

Today, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services is failing these hundreds of thousands of young people, as renewals stall and Congress continues to put off action.  

Every DACA holder must renew his or her status every two years to keep working legally. If that renewal isn’t processed on time, employers must let the workers go as soon as their permits lapse. DACA recipients, who are required to have been in the country since at least June 15, 2007, lose protection at that point from deportation.   

The delays have gotten measurably worse in the past year. DACA renewal applications, which took an average of two weeks to process in fiscal 2025, now take four to six months, with one in five recipients waiting more than seven months. Citizenship and Immigration Services has completed roughly 40 percent fewer renewals in fiscal 2026 than it had at this point in 2025.  

This isn’t a policy debate anymore. It’s machinery of government breaking down in real time, and hundreds of thousands of people are caught in the gears.  

Because of the increasing delays, the DACA population has shrunk by roughly 100,000 people since January 2025, falling from 533,000 at the beginning of 2025 to 436,000 in June 2026. These individuals are falling out of status through no fault of their own. They are stuck waiting on paperwork.

A program that exists to keep people in the workforce is now doing the opposite: stripping status from people through procedural delays. Employers can lose trained staff with no warning; families lose income overnight. People who are here legally can be deported without warning. None of this reflects any change in eligibility or any new finding about a person’s record, but an agency that cannot keep pace with its own caseload.  

The current administration, once threatening to end the program entirely, notably has not done so; one has to wonder whether these delays are a means to end the program by attrition.  Regardless, legislation would end the instability for good.  

This group of people has been vetted more than any other group of immigrants in the United States. Every one of them has already been fingerprinted, background-checked and re-vetted every two years since the program began. Nearly 90 percent of all DACA recipients are employed, paying taxes and building lives in the only country most of them remember. If the renewal issues persist, the American workforce will lose tens of thousands of skilled workers. Moreover, most of them have families, and yet are limited in how much they can really contribute to the country by the very temporariness of their status.  

Both Republicans and Democrats, including President Trump, have called on Congress to create a permanent solution for these people. It’s time for them to put their votes where their statements are and pass the DREAM Act, or any of several other pieces of bipartisan legislation that have been proposed over the last 20 years.   

Fourteen years of the DACA program isn’t a milestone to be celebrated. It’s evidence of a failure of Congress to act on an issue they have said they want to fix. Maybe it’s just one of many areas they have failed to act upon, but this one has human consequences. 

Theresa Cardinal Brown has worked for more than 30 years in immigration law, policy and practice. She served in policy roles at U.S. Customs and Border Protection and the Department of Homeland Security during the George W. Bush and Barack Obama administrations, and is currently a fellow at the National Immigration Forum and a leader in the Council on National Security and Immigration.

data.title: Military says it disabled vessel that 'attempted to run the U.S. naval blockade' against Iran
data.description:
American forces on Thursday disabled a commercial vessel attempting to bypass the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, U.S. Central Command (Centcom) said Friday.

The crew of the bulk carrier “attempted to run the U.S. naval blockade, despite multiple warnings” after departing the southern port city of Bandar Abbas, Iran, Centcom said in a release.

“A U.S. military aircraft launched precision munitions that struck the stern of Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer,” the command added. “The ship’s propulsion was ultimately disabled and the civilian crew was unharmed.”

Centcom also shared an unclassified, 8 second video of a munition striking the vessel.

American forces resumed blockading Iranian ports in the middle of July, after previously do so from mid-April until late June amid the U.S. and Israeli war on Iran.

Adm. Brad Cooper, the commander of Centcom, said on Oct. 16 that the blockade had cost the Islamic Republic $25 billion in oil revenue — directly impacting the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

“As a point of emphasis, with the exception of the humanitarian assistance we’ve allowed in, Iran has no exports and no imports by sea,” Cooper said in a video. “The sum total of these actions has imposed devastating costs on Iran’s security apparatus and the IRGC specifically.”

Centcom marked 130 consecutive days of the blockade last weekend, writing on the social platform X it is “preventing” the IRGC “from exporting billions of dollars in crude oil.”

The command said Friday its forces have “redirected” 158 compliant commercial vessels and “disabled” six others that refused to comply with the blockade. 

“All mariners operating in the Gulf of Oman and approaches to the Strait of Hormuz are urged to heed blockade warnings issued by CENTCOM forces,” the command added.

The Iran war will hit the nine-month mark on Saturday. President Trump said Thursday the conflict will end “sort of whenever” he decides to wind it down.

During a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing on Nov. 13, Pentagon budget official Arthur Miller told Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) that the conflict had cost taxpayers $48.3 billion.

The figure included munitions costs, equipment replacement costs and operational costs, but did not account for total damage to U.S. military facilities in the Middle East by Iranian forces, Miller noted.

data.title: 5 big questions for Democrats this Thanksgiving
data.description:
Democrats are entering the last month of the year on a high.

The midterm election results surpassed all but the most optimistic expectations for the party. Even six months ago, the idea of the Democrats racking up a net gain of nine seats in the Senate would have seemed implausible. Their final House majority will have a margin of greater than 80 seats.

The outcome has given the opposition party the leverage to investigate President Trump’s actions and to constrain any new legislative moves that he might make.

Black Friday-Cyber Monday Deals

  • Black Friday deals are live: Apple, Dyson, Ninja and more
  • Amazon’s Black Friday sale is live with some of the lowest prices this year
  • 40+ Black Friday deals at their lowest price this year

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

At the same time, Democrats face challenges of their own, including how to navigate internal tensions and how to best prioritize their next moves.

Here are five questions facing the Democratic Party this Thanksgiving.

Can they get stuff done on affordability?

The Democratic victory in the midterms was fueled in significant part by voter discontent over the cost of living — and a perception that Trump and the GOP had failed to address the problem.

Now the onus will be on Democrats to take action and show progress.

Soon-to-be-Speaker Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) outlined in a recent interview with Lulu Garcia-Navarro of The New York Times how his party might go about this. 

Jeffries said that Democrats would seek to revoke the massive cuts to Medicaid and to SNAP benefits that were part of Trump’s so-called Big Beautiful Bill. The GOP legislation is projected to cut around $1 trillion from Medicaid and around $186 billion from SNAP over the next decade.

Jeffries also suggested Democrats would seek to roll back the Trump tariffs that many economists believe have added to inflationary pressures, even as the president insists otherwise.

A larger unknown is what will happen with the war on Iran, which has caused energy prices to rise. Democrats could try to force an end to the conflict, perhaps trying to choke off funding. But Trump remains as unpredictable as ever on the topic.

There is another political question on affordability, too. If public perception in 12 or 18 months is that the cost of living remains unacceptably high, how will blame be doled out among the Democrats and Trump?

How will they manage tensions between the left and center-left?

Before the midterms triumph, Democrats had a rather fraught primary season, with challengers on the progressive left facing off against more establishment-friendly, centrist rivals.

The left did not prevail everywhere, but it saw some big victories. Most prominently, Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D) vanquished Rep. Haley Stevens (D) in the primary before defeating former Rep. Mike Rogers (R) in the general election. 

There were other examples, too, including primary victories over Democratic incumbents for leftist figures such as Melat Kiros in Colorado and Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York. Kiros and Chevalier, both of whom easily won their general election races, are members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).

The progressive candidates capitalized in part on a sense among parts of the Democratic base that party leadership has been too timid in fighting back against Trump, and too unambitious in its policy prescriptions. The issue of Israel and the Palestinians is also a visceral one.

Even so, numerous centrist office-holders are wary of the progressives, fearing that the left’s ideas have less appeal in electoral battlegrounds than among primary voters.

The internal debates aren’t about to end anytime soon. They could burn even hotter once Democrats take the reins of power on Capitol Hill.

When does the 2028 field start forming?

The left-vs-center tensions will infuse the race for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028 as well.

A number of significant figures are publicly contemplating running. None has yet made an official declaration, but someone will fire the starting pistol soon enough.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) is seen by most as almost certain to run. Less clear is whether 2024 nominee and former Vice President Kamala Harris will try again, or whether Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) will enter the fray.

A potential Ocasio-Cortez run is especially intriguing because, if she goes for it, she is likely to be the undisputed standard-bearer of the left. If Ocasio-Cortez passes on a bid, several other candidates could seek the progressive mantle.

The centrist faction in the party will get representation in the presidential field too, especially if the likes of Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear or former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel run.

How does Van Hollen do in his challenge to Schumer?

This is the question of the moment inside the Beltway.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) is accruing at least some support as he seeks to defeat the long-standing Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer (D-N.Y. ) as the party prepares to take the majority in the upper chamber.

Van Hollen is just nine years younger than the 76-year-old Schumer and hardly a hard-left figure. But he is positioning himself as the option for those who want more progressive leadership — including on the Israel-Palestine question — or who are pressing for generational change.

The Maryland senator has received public support from progressives including El-Sayed, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Sen-elect Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) and, on Wednesday, Sen.-elect Troy Jackson (D-Maine). 

But not all his backers are in the left-wing camp. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) is also among Van Hollen’s supporters.

Schumer remains the favorite to win the leadership contest, and his loyalists question why the party would throw him overboard after such a successful election cycle.

Still, the final vote will be an important barometer of satisfaction, or dissatisfaction, with Schumer and with party leadership more generally. 

How hard will they go after Trump?

Incoming House Oversight Committee Chair Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) had a message for Republicans as the results rolled in on Election Night: “Lawyer up,” he wrote on social media.

It’s clear that Democrats will launch several investigations into the Trump administration. Their base will not settle for anything less, especially given the sheer numbers and scale of Trump-related controversies.

At the same time, some strategists worry that a focus on Trump is not necessarily the most effective gambit as the party seeks to consolidate its 2026 victories and win the White House in 2028.

Others argue it is perfectly feasible for Democrats to take a twin-track approach, seeking both to hold Trump and his allies accountable while advancing policies on kitchen-table issues.

data.title: Portnoy says Vance 'done' as 2028 presidential contender
data.description:
Barstool Sports founder Dave Portnoy, who has used his large social media following to promote President Trump, said Vice President Vance has no chance of winning the White House in 2028.

During an interview on “The Scott Jennings Show” on Tuesday, Portnoy told the conservative commentator that he favored Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) as the GOP nominee.

“I like the way he’s run Florida. Like, I’m here, it’s the only state that turned red, stayed red, barely, and I think he’s pretty good,” Portnoy said, after Jennings asked if he preferred Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

“I would go Rubio over — I think this: I think JD’s done. Like, I don’t think he has a chance. I think he’s too closely affiliated with Trump,” Portnoy said.

“And I also, I don’t know how you go — he’s going to have to distance himself from Trump, and I don’t know how you go from ‘Trump was the worst’ to ‘Trump was the best’ back to ‘Trump was not so good,’ which he would have to do to win,” he added.

The GOP faced a walloping in this year’s midterms, with the Democrats taking back the House and Senate, even winning in places where the party has historically struggled, like Texas and Kansas.

Trump’s approval rating was at record lows ahead of Election Day, and was sitting at 35.80 percent on Friday morning, according to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, with his disapproval rating at 61.6 percent.

Talk of a potential Rubio bid in 2028 has recently heated up, while enthusiasm for Vance has cooled in the wake of the midterms.

Vance emerged from the midterms blaming the Iran war for the GOP drubbing, and declined to say whether he supported Trump’s decision to launch the war when asked last week.

The headwinds facing any Republican nominee in 2028 has spurred speculation that Vance may wait out the upcoming election.

Portnoy spoke to NPR in July about his new book, noting the “manosphere” had largely turned on Trump over the Iran war.

He told NPR last year that his support for Trump in 2024 was more “an indictment of the Democrats than an endorsement of Trump’s politics.”

He also said he had a less hardline view on immigration.

“I don’t necessarily think you should go back in time,” he told NPR. “If somebody isn’t here legally, but they’re a productive member of society with no issues, I don’t think that you go say, ‘Get out of here.'”

Trump hasn’t backed a successor, suggesting last week that chief of staff Stephen Miller could make a good president.

DeSantis is among a handful of governors seen as potential 2028 contenders, along with outgoing Gov. Brian Kemp of Georgia and former Gov. Glenn Youngkin of Virginia. Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas) is also seen as a likely candidate.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.
